newsitem.title: USA: Heir sells 9 million shares for $720 million.
newsitem.headline: Heir sells 9 million shares for $720 million.

text.p: John Dorrance III, the grandson of the founder of Campbell Soup Co., said he sold Campbell stock worth at least $769 million Thursday, much of it in one of the single biggest trades ever on the New York Stock Exchange.

Dorrance said in a Securities and Exchange Commission filing that he sold more than 9.6 million shares at $80 to $81.125 a share, and much of that was in one blockbuster trade of 9 million shares that crossed the tape just after midday.

Dorrance has been selling Campbell stock this year in a bid to cash in on the strength of the shares. The company's stock has been rising on its improving earnings and after it announced a major restructuring and stock buyback programme on Sept. 5, the stock has jumped further.

Analysts noted that the sales by Dorrance -- which cut his holdings this year to about 5.4 million shares, or just over 2 percent of Campbell's stock, from almost 27 million -- came near all-time high prices for the shares.
The sales raised no red flags about Campbell's earnings performance, other than underscoring that the stock is no longer a bargain, they said.

The challenge facing the grandson of the man who developed condensed soup was not how to remove water to make a better product, but how to liquiditate a portfolio that was overflowing with inherited Campbell Soup stock.

"Obviously, he thinks the stock at 80 is better than 40, but seriously, it is a statement by a knowledgable insider that he doesn't think the stock is cheap anymore," said William Leach at Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette.

"The stock has had a big run-up recently," he said, having risen about 15 points since the company announced on Sept. 5 that it would sell low-margin businesses and cut 650 jobs, or about 2.6 percent of its work force, and buy back $2 billion of stock.
Dorrance, an avid racing fan who owns a number of horses, was not available for comment. He resigned from Campbell's board of directors last year and became an Irish citizen.
Campbell said it was not involved in the single 9-million-share trade, which crossed at $80 a share, off $3 from Wednesday's closing price, on the New York Stock Exchange at 12:32 p.m. EST.

J.P. Morgan & Co. Inc. handled the trade and probably lined up the buyers, Wall Street sources said. The soup and food company, based in Camden, N.J., said the buyers included a "number of leading growth-oriented institutions."
The NYSE said the trade was the seventh biggest block trade in dollar terms ever on the exchange, and the largest in 3-1/2 years.

A Campbell spokesman said Dorrance's holdings came entirely from a generation-skipping trust established by the company founder and that Dorrance assumed ownership of the shares when his father died. Such steps are usually meant to lessen the tax burden for future generations.

Dorrance led a highly publicised debate among heirs to the soup fortune over their role in the company after the death of his father, John T. Dorrance Jr., in 1989. He was a prominent and successful advocate of retaining family control.
The Campbell spokesman said the company has not had any contact with Dorrance since he resigned from the board. Two of his siblings and two cousins remain on the 15-member board.

In filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Oct. 7 and Oct. 10 detailing previous stock sales, he said he would sell more shares as opportunities arose, and he repeated that in the filing on Thursday.
Campbell stock fell $3 to close at $80 on the New York Stock Exchange where volume of 10.3 million shares made it the most active issue.
